content: The title of the physical examination page should be formatted as (Disease name) physical examination, with only the first letter of the title capitalized. The purpose of this section is to provide a detailed description of the various aspects of the physical examination, with a focus on how the disease in question may present. This section is not intended to explain how to perform a physical examination unless specialized signs are included (e.g., Chvostek's sign). In such cases, a brief description of the sign may be provided. For example, in appendicitis, physical examination findings may include right lower quadrant abdominal tenderness. Unique findings may also suggest specific aspects or complications of the disease. For instance, rebound tenderness in appendicitis may indicate peritonitis. At the top of the edit box, include the {{CMG}} template, your name template, and the microchapter navigation template you created. Ensure that links within the page are created by placing brackets around key terms to link to other pages. These links should be as specific as possible. For example, if the phrase anterior spinal artery syndrome appears, the link should direct to anterior spinal artery syndrome rather than generic terms like anterior, artery, or syndrome. For more information on creating links, click here. Follow the formatting and capitalization guidelines outlined in the template. Below are examples of what to include in the physical examination section. Overview The overview section should begin with the disease name in the first sentence. The goal is to summarize the physical examination page in a few sentences. This section can mirror the physical examination segment on the overview page. For an example of an overview section, click here. Template First Sentences Examples of preferred template statements include: Patients with [disease] usually appear [description]. Physical examination of patients with [disease] is usually remarkable for [findings]. Common physical examination findings of [disease] include [findings]. The presence of [finding] on physical examination is diagnostic of [disease]. The presence of [finding] on physical examination is highly suggestive of [disease]. Physical Examination Appearance of the Patient This section should provide a general description of the typical appearance of a patient with the disease. If patients typically appear normal, you may write, Patients are usually well-appearing. Physical descriptions such as obese, thin, cachectic, ill-appearing, or diaphoretic may also be included. For example, patients may appear well-appearing in the early stages of cancer but cachectic in the late stages. For an example of this section, click here. Vital Signs Vital signs traditionally include temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate. Additional parameters such as oxygen saturation (on room air) and blood glucose levels may also be included. HEENT (Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Throat) Abnormalities in this section may include: Evidence of trauma Icteric sclera Nystagmus Abnormal extraocular movements Pupils that are non-reactive to light, accommodation, or both Abnormal findings on ophthalmoscopic examination Reduced hearing acuity Abnormal Weber test (Note: A positive Weber test is considered normal, while a negative Weber test is abnormal. To avoid confusion, you may write abnormal Weber test.) Abnormal Rinne test (Note: A positive Rinne test is considered normal, while a negative Rinne test is abnormal. To avoid confusion, you may write abnormal Rinne test.) Genitourinary Findings in this section may include: A palpable pelvic or adnexal mass Inflamed mucosa Clear or colored, foul-smelling or odorless penile or vaginal discharge Pathognomonic findings such as discharge resembling cottage cheese in Candida albicans vulvovaginitis or a fishy odor in bacterial vaginosis.
